lines: A load test comes back reporting a perfectly respectable average latency.
And in that very same run, one real shopper sat there waiting a full several seconds for their page to load.
One tidy average. One real person who waited far, far longer than that average ever suggested.
So which numbers would have actually surfaced that gap, the one the average quietly buried.
And just as importantly, which way of generating the test's own load would have even caught that slow request in the first place.
answer: The full ladder of percentiles catches it, especially out near its far tail.

But only if the load generator itself paces its requests on a steady, constant schedule. A generator that waits politely for each response before sending the next one would have simply never sent a request during that slow stretch, so nothing about it ever gets measured at all.

lines: Here's why an average so easily hides a tail like that.
One rare, genuinely large stall gets diluted across every other ordinary request sitting around it in the same batch.
Spread thin enough across a big enough pile of ordinary numbers, that one outlier barely nudges the average at all.
Picture five distinct points sitting along that same one distribution.

Each one is honestly answering a genuinely different real question. The typical request. A somewhat unlucky user. A genuinely very unlucky one. Something rare enough that it only shows up once you have real volume. And finally, the single worst request this entire run ever saw.
Take two separate hosts, each reporting its own tail percentile honestly.
Average those two numbers together, and that average quietly disagrees with the true tail percentile of their actual combined traffic.
Histograms themselves add together cleanly. Percentiles computed from them never do.
On its own, one single server's own rare tail moment is genuinely unlikely.
Now fan that same request out across a great many such servers running in parallel.
The odds flip hard, because the single slowest one among all of them is what actually sets the whole request's latency.
Run two different load generators side by side, at the exact same offered load, with the exact same stall dropped into both.
One generator politely waits for each response before sending its next request. The other keeps marching along on a fixed, steady schedule no matter what.
The polite one's own reported tail stays looking calm and healthy. The steady one honestly reports the entire backlog that stall actually caused.
Pulling this together now.

An average genuinely hides a tail. The full percentile ladder answers five separate real questions, never just one. Histograms merge cleanly together. Percentiles computed from them simply do not average that same way.
And fanning a request out across many servers multiplies tail risk, rather than smoothing it away.
A whole fleet of ten separate hosts each independently reports its own tail percentile as exactly the same number.
Does that mean the fleet's own combined tail percentile is automatically that same number too.
answer: Ten hosts quietly agreeing on their own separate numbers tells you remarkably little about the real shape of their combined traffic once it's all merged together.
The only honest way to know the fleet's true combined number is to actually merge all ten histograms and read the real percentile straight off of that merge.
